Exemptions from Making Tax Digital for Income Tax: who's automatically exempt, and how to apply if you're digitally excluded

By Daniel Wyatt · Facts checked 21 November 2026

Short answer: some people are exempt from Making Tax Digital for Income Tax automatically (for example, qualifying income of £20,000 or less, or no National Insurance number before the tax year starts), and HMRC doesn't need to hear from them. Others have to apply, most often because they're digitally excluded: it isn't reasonable for them to use software because of age, health, disability, location or religious beliefs. You apply by phone or letter, and GOV.UK says HMRC won't accept an application whose only reason is unfamiliarity with software, having few records, or the extra time or cost.

Everything on this page comes from GOV.UK pages we read on 21 November 2026, linked under each section. The main exemptions page was last updated on 12 November 2026. Where GOV.UK doesn't say something, we say so.

At a glance

TypeDo you contact HMRC?Examples (GOV.UK)How long it lasts
Automatic, permanentNoQualifying income £20,000 or less; no National Insurance number before the tax year; trusts (SA900), non-resident companies (SA700) and personal representatives; Lloyd's members (SA103L); not physically or mentally capable with a power of attorney or deputy in placeUnless your circumstances change
Automatic, temporaryNoOn your 2024 to 2025 return: averaging relief (SA103 or SA104), qualifying care relief, the SA107 or SA109 pagesUntil April 2027
Automatic, beyond April 2027NoOn your 2024 to 2025 return: ministers of religion (SA102M), Married Couple's Allowance (born before 6 April 1935), Blind Person's AllowanceUntil HMRC sets a timeline
Apply: digitally excludedYesAge, health or disability; religious beliefs; no internet access at home, work or a suitable alternative placeMay be permanent, depending on circumstances
Apply: temporary or beyond April 2027YesThe same claims or pages as above, if they weren't on your 2024 to 2025 return but you reasonably expect them on your 2025 to 2026 or 2026 to 2027 returnAs for the matching automatic exemption
PartnershipsNoPartnerships don't currently need to use MTD for Income TaxUntil HMRC sets a timeline

Whatever the type, GOV.UK says that if you're exempt you still send a Self Assessment tax return as normal.

Source: GOV.UK, Find out if you can get an exemption from Making Tax Digital for Income Tax.

Automatic exemptions in more detail

  • £20,000 or less. Qualifying income (self-employment and property income before expenses) of £20,000 or less means you're automatically exempt. The thresholds that bring people in are over £50,000 (from 6 April 2026), over £30,000 (from 6 April 2027) and over £20,000 (from 6 April 2028). See Do I need MTD, and when?
  • No National Insurance number. You're exempt, and can't sign up, if you don't have one before the start of the tax year. GOV.UK's example: someone who gets their number on 30 April 2026 with qualifying income over £50,000 for 2024 to 2025 is exempt for 2026 to 2027.
  • Acting for someone else. Trusts sending an SA900, non-resident companies sending an SA700, and personal representatives of someone who has died are exempt in that role. GOV.UK points out that your own self-employment or property income may still bring you into MTD.
  • Not able to deal with HMRC yourself. You're exempt if your 2024 to 2025 return said you're not physically or mentally capable of providing information to HMRC and you have a power of attorney in place for someone in the UK, or a legally appointed deputy, controller or guardian.
  • Temporary, until April 2027. If your 2024 to 2025 return claimed averaging relief (farmers, market gardeners and people who personally create literary or artistic works), qualifying care relief (for example foster or kinship carers), or included the SA107 (trusts and estates) or SA109 pages, you don't need MTD for 2026 to 2027. GOV.UK says you'll need it from 2027 to 2028 if your qualifying income is above £30,000 in 2025 to 2026. On 12 November 2026 GOV.UK updated this to say averaging relief claimed on the SA104 (partnership) page also counts automatically.
  • Beyond April 2027. Ministers of religion (SA102M), Lloyd's members (SA103L), and people who declared they received or transferred Married Couple's Allowance or Blind Person's Allowance. GOV.UK says these people will need to use MTD in the future, with a timeline to come.

Source: GOV.UK, Find out if you can get an exemption; thresholds from GOV.UK, Find out if and when you need to use MTD for Income Tax.

What "digitally excluded" means to HMRC

GOV.UK says being digitally excluded means it's not reasonable for you to use compatible software to keep digital records, or to send quarterly updates or your tax return. Its examples:

GOV.UK gives as possible reasonsGOV.UK says isn't enough on its own
Your age, health condition or disability stops you using a computer, tablet or smartphone to keep digital records or submit themYou previously filed a paper return
You're a practising member of a religious society or order whose beliefs are incompatible with digital communications or records, and you don't use a computer, tablet or smartphone for business or personal useYou're unfamiliar with accountancy software
You can't get internet access at home or at your business because of your location, and can't get access at a suitable alternative locationYou have a small number of digital records to create each year
It will take extra time or cost to sign up and use MTD

Points worth knowing:

  • Age alone isn't listed. Age appears only where it stops you using a device. GOV.UK gives no age cut-off.
  • Case by case. GOV.UK says there may be other reasons you are or aren't digitally excluded, and HMRC considers every application individually.
  • It's about you, not your helper. If an agent, friend or family member applies for you, the decision is still based on your personal circumstances.
  • If an agent does your tax. GOV.UK says an agent who uses compatible software and submits your records can meet MTD's requirements for you, so you may not need a digitally excluded exemption at all.
  • Already exempt from MTD for VAT? If HMRC confirmed you're digitally excluded for VAT, GOV.UK says to contact Self Assessment general enquiries with your National Insurance number, VAT registration number and the reason, and say whether your circumstances have changed. If they haven't, HMRC will confirm you're also exempt for Income Tax; if they have, you apply as normal. A VAT exemption because of insolvency doesn't carry over if you're already signed up for MTD for Income Tax.

Sources: GOV.UK, Find out if you can get an exemption; GOV.UK, Apply for an exemption from MTD for Income Tax.

When to apply

GOV.UK says to apply before you need to start using MTD. For a digitally excluded exemption it gives these timings:

If you need to use MTD from…GOV.UK says
6 April 2026 (over £50,000 in 2024 to 2025)You can apply now
6 April 2027 (over £30,000 in 2025 to 2026)You can apply now
6 April 2028 (over £20,000 in 2026 to 2027)Apply from summer 2027 onwards

If you've already signed up and your circumstances change, GOV.UK says to apply and keep using MTD while you wait for a decision. If you think you might qualify for more than one exemption, GOV.UK says to send a single application explaining why each one applies.

Source: GOV.UK, Apply for an exemption from MTD for Income Tax.

How to apply

GOV.UK describes phone or letter only; it doesn't mention an online form.

  • Yourself, or a friend or family member: call or write using HMRC's Self Assessment: general enquiries contact details. That page lists 0300 200 3310 (Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm, closed bank holidays) and the address Self Assessment, HM Revenue and Customs, BX9 1AS, United Kingdom.
  • Agents: use the Agent Dedicated Line: Self Assessment or PAYE for individuals, and apply for each client individually.
  • Letter titles: "Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — digitally excluded application", or "Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — exemption application" for any other exemption.
  • Friends and family need the person's authorisation first: either in writing to HMRC with the person's signature, or by phone with the person there to give it verbally.
  • If contacting HMRC is hard because of a health condition or your circumstances, see Get help from HMRC if you need extra support.

What GOV.UK says to include

ItemWhen
National Insurance number, name and address (of the applicant)Every application
Why you think you (or they) should be exempt, with any supporting informationEvery application
How you're connected to the applicant (for example agent or personal representative)Applying for someone else
How the tax return is sent now, including if someone else helpsDigitally excluded
The reason for being digitally excluded, with supporting informationDigitally excluded
Whether there's an agent (for example an accountant) and what they'll doDigitally excluded
Any additional needs, so HMRC can give the right supportDigitally excluded

GOV.UK says HMRC may ask for more information. It doesn't list specific documents that count as supporting information.

Sources: GOV.UK, Apply for an exemption from MTD for Income Tax; GOV.UK, Self Assessment: general enquiries (read 21 November 2026).

After you apply

  1. Decision time: HMRC aims to respond within 28 calendar days of receiving your application, longer if it needs more information. It may check the information you gave.
  2. While you wait: GOV.UK suggests reading the steps for MTD so you're ready to sign up if the application isn't accepted, and says to keep records and supporting documents as you normally do for Self Assessment.
  3. If accepted: the letter says what type of exemption you have and how long it lasts. An exemption until April 2027 means you won't need to sign up until the 2027 to 2028 tax year at the earliest. While you're exempt in 2026 to 2027, you stay on the current Self Assessment late filing and late payment penalties (more in our MTD penalties guide).
  4. If refused: the letter explains why and how to appeal. You can appeal up to 30 days after the date on the letter, in writing to the address in the letter, titled "Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — digitally excluded appeal" or "Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — exemption appeal", with any new information. If you need more time, GOV.UK says to contact Self Assessment general enquiries (or the Agent Dedicated Line for agents).

Source: GOV.UK, Apply for an exemption from MTD for Income Tax; GOV.UK, Penalties for MTD for Income Tax.

If an exemption isn't available

The other routes GOV.UK describes are using MTD-compatible software yourself, or having an agent keep digital records and submit them for you. If you're looking at software, these pages may help:

  • Can I keep using spreadsheets? Bridging software and digital links
  • Free MTD software: what's really free, and the catches
  • Compare all HMRC-recognised software

What GOV.UK doesn't say

  • What specific evidence HMRC expects with a digitally excluded application: not listed.
  • Whether there's an age at which HMRC treats someone as digitally excluded: none is given.
  • When the "beyond April 2027" groups and partnerships will need to start: GOV.UK says it will set out a timeline later.

Quick answers

Can I get an exemption from Making Tax Digital because of my age?

Not because of age alone. GOV.UK lists age as one possible reason for being digitally excluded, but only where your age, health condition or disability stops you from using a computer, tablet or smartphone to keep digital records or send them to HMRC. GOV.UK doesn't give an age cut-off. HMRC considers each application case by case.

Is there an online form to apply for an MTD exemption?

No online form is mentioned. GOV.UK says to apply by phone or in writing using the Self Assessment: general enquiries contact details (agents use the Agent Dedicated Line). Letters should be titled 'Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — digitally excluded application' or 'Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — exemption application'.

What reasons will HMRC not accept?

GOV.UK says HMRC won't accept an application if your only reason is that you previously filed a paper return, you're unfamiliar with accountancy software, you have a small number of digital records each year, or it will take extra time or cost to sign up and use MTD.

How long does HMRC take to decide?

GOV.UK says HMRC aims to respond within 28 calendar days of receiving your application, and it may take longer if HMRC needs more information. It then writes to say whether the application is accepted, what type of exemption it is and how long it lasts.

Can I appeal if HMRC refuses my exemption?

Yes. GOV.UK says the decision letter explains why and how to appeal, and you can appeal up to 30 days after the date on the letter. Appeals are in writing, to the address in the letter, titled 'Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — digitally excluded appeal' or 'Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — exemption appeal'.

If I'm exempt, do I still file a tax return?

Yes. GOV.UK says that if you're exempt you don't have to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, but you must continue to report your income and gains in a Self Assessment tax return as normal.

Do I need an exemption if an accountant does my tax?

Possibly not. GOV.UK says that if your agent uses compatible software to keep digital records and submits them to HMRC, they can meet the MTD requirements on your behalf, so you may not need to apply for a digitally excluded exemption. GOV.UK suggests speaking to your agent about this.
